paragraphs: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Ela (another version: ben Elazar). In [Pesachim 113b](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.113b.18) they said: “He is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Tavla, he is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakla, he is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Ela (another version: Elazar).” Hyman describes the reading cited in Yuchasin HaShalem as precious and true: “Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Tavla; he is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakula; he is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar,” and explains that these are two matters, that is, that Rabbi

Yitzchak Nappacha is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Tavla, and Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakula is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar; and so the reading is cited in Dikdukei Soferim there, note ק (qof), from manuscript א״פ. Hyman continues: I have already discussed at length in the entry Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha that this is the truth, and I will bring here proof that Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakula is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar: in [Jerusalem Talmud Ketubot, chapter 13, end of halakhah 1](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Ketubot.13.1.7), “Rabbi Ba bar Zavda in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chakula: Wherever we learned,

‘Rabban Gamliel said: I see the words of Admon,’ the halakhah is likewise.” In the parallel at [Ketubot 109a](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.109a.5): Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar transmits the rule in Chizkiyah’s name: “Wherever we learned, ‘Rabban Gamliel said: I see the words of Admon,’ the halakhah follows him.”[^9] Hyman argues that Rabbi Abba bar Zavda speaking in his name does not mean that he was his student, but that he had traditions from Chizkiyah and transmitted them to Rabbi Abba bar Zavda. Likewise we find in [Jerusalem Talmud Orlah 1:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Orlah.1.2.9), “Rabbi Yitzchak

bar Chakuli in the name of Chizkiyah,” and in [Ketubot 109a](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.109a.5) and Avodah Zarah 45a in Hyman’s citation (compare [Avodah Zarah 48b:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Avodah_Zarah.48b.7)), “Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar in Chizkiyah’s name.”[^11] He likewise had traditions from the Amoraim of the first generation, as we find that he spoke in the name of Rabbi Yehudah Nesia (I in Hyman’s designation), as in Jerusalem Talmud Ketubot 2:9 and Jerusalem Talmud Gittin 3:4; and in Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin 7:10, “Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakula in the name of Rabbi Yudan Nesiya.” In the name of Rabbi Hoshaya:

as in Gittin, beginning of chapter 8; in the name of Rabbi Yannai, Yoma, beginning of chapter 4. He likewise had traditions in the name of Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi (who lived longer than his brother Rabban Gamliel, as explained in his entry), as at the end of Jerusalem Talmud Sukkah, chapter 1, and Jerusalem Talmud Ketubot 2:7: “Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chakula: Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi ruled regarding these at the entrance,” etc. (Penei Moshe there explains that Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakuli and Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi both ruled, which Hyman considers an error.)

Likewise we find in Jerusalem Talmud Peah 1:4 and Jerusalem Talmud Nedarim 8:1: “Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakuli and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi both say,” etc.; Hyman considers it undoubted that this does not make him a colleague of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, but that both said the same thing. At the end of Rabbi Yochanan’s days he was already the leading sage of the generation, as we find in [Moed Katan 25b:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Moed_Katan.25b.10): when Rabbi Yochanan died, Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar eulogized him, opening: “This day is as hard for Israel as the day the sun set at noon.”

In fact he was friendly with all of Rabbi Yochanan’s great students, as in [Moed Katan 20a:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Moed_Katan.20a.10): “Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha sat at the gate of Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar.” In [Eruvin 54b:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin.54b.4) Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar relates of Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat when he was in Tzippori (this was when he came to the Land of Israel and studied then before Rabbi Chanina) that once a man came to take his garment and found a viper in it.

Now in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot, chapter 1, end of halakhah 5, Hyman finds a wondrous thing: “Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar raised an objection before Rabbi Yose: Since you say [that blessings follow] their concluding formulas, one does not say a biblical verse as a blessing. They said: This young man is wise, for he understands. What does ‘after their concluding formulas’ mean? That if one was standing in morning prayer, forgot and mentioned the evening text, and returned and concluded with the morning text, he has fulfilled [his obligation].” Hyman asks how Rabbi Yose could call him

“this child.” Although we find that Rabbi Yochanan said so of Resh Lakish in Me’ilah 7b — “I cut off the child’s feet” — even though he was then already the leading sage of the generation, a student-colleague of Rabbi Yochanan, Hyman prefers the reading of the Jerusalem Talmud at the supplied locator Taanit פ״ה ה״ג [5:3; see note], where it reads: “They said: So is this matter.” And so the reading is in the Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot, Constantinople printing: “Rabbi Yitzchak bar Elazar raised an objection before Rabbi Yasa

… they said: So is this matter,” etc. Hyman suggests that in his old age he went to Caesarea and was under the shadow of Rabbi Abbahu. This is what we find in Jerusalem Talmud Demai 2:1 (the printed locator reads פ״ב ה״א־ו.): “Rabbi Mana said: I went to Caesarea … I asked Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar, and he said to me: Zuga (זוגא) used to treat it as permitted (שוריי)” [see note], “Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar in the name of Zuga of Caesarea.” Likewise we find that Rabbi Abbahu spoke in his name, as in Jerusalem Talmud Bava Batra 10:1.

We find in [Yoma 78a:12-13](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.78a.12-13): “Rabbi Tzadok ben Chaluka stood on his feet and said: I saw Rabbi Yose ben Zimra … Rabbi Abba said to him: The incident was not so,” etc. Hyman reports finding the name Rabbi Tzadok ben Chaluka nowhere else, but regards the reading of Yuchasin and Dikdukei Soferim as more correct: “Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chakulah stood on his feet … and Rabbi Abbahu said to him” (and the word Chakulah is also in the Venice printing and the other

old printings). Hyman suggests that, since he afterward lived in Caesarea, he was called by this name, as in Tanchuma, Behaalotekha 16: “Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar of Caesarea said: What wisdom made a crown for its head, humility made a sandal for its foot.” The saying is cited in the Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, chapter 1, end of halakhah 3, and there simply “Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar said”; and this is as Hyman argues, that Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar without further designation is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar of Caesarea.

He is mentioned in halakhah in [Sukkah 35b:14](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.35b.14) and [Yevamot 65b:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.65b.2). He had students who were great men of the generation, as we find in [Shabbat 29b:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.29b.7): “Avin of Tzippori dragged a bench in a marble upper chamber in front of Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar; he said to him,” etc. Rabbi Hoshaya bar Shimi was his student, as in Jerusalem Talmud Kilayim 6:3: “Rabbi Mana said: I went to Caesarea and heard Rabbi Hoshaya bar Shimi in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak ben

Elazar”; and in Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat, chapter 11, end of halakhah 5, and Jerusalem Talmud Moed Katan 2:3: “Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar instructed Rabbi Hoshaya bar Shimi.” Likewise Rabbi Mani, as above. Rabbi Yesi ben Yesi in his name: the end of Jerusalem Talmud Terumot, chapter 1. Rabbi Shmuel bar Avdimi asked him: Jerusalem Talmud Shabbat 19:1. Rabbi Tanchuma in his name: Jerusalem Talmud Bikkurim 1:3.

His precious sayings in aggadah: what we brought above from the Jerusalem Talmud [Shabbat], 1, end of halakhah 3: “What wisdom made a crown for its head, humility made a heel for its sandal.” In [Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 7:3:9](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Berakhot.7.3.9) and [Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 3:7:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Megillah.3.7.6), his precious saying: “The prophets knew that their God is true, and they do not flatter Him.”[^10] Hyman cites Yoma 79b (compare [Yoma 69b:16](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.69b.16)) for the saying and argues that the words “Rabbi Yitzchak ben” are missing, leaving only

“Rabbi Elazar”; in Midrash Tehillim it reads “Rabbi Yaakov son of Rabbi Elazar”; Hyman proposes that the written ר״י here denotes Rabbi Yitzchak. In Jerusalem Talmud Maaser Sheni, chapter 5, end of halakhah 3, he said (by way of a popular proverb): “At a meal (בשרותא, in Hyman’s reading) it requires filling; the sava (סבא) of the wood is from itself and in itself” (Jerusalem Talmud Beitzah 2:4 reads “the sama (סמא) of the wood is from itself and in itself”); “any coal that does not burn at once does not burn.” The commentators went far afield;

Hyman’s own interpretation is: to me it seems, according to its plain sense, along the lines of what they said in Eichah Rabbah 3:66, “Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar knew how to arrange his meal according to the number of the days of the solar year”: what he said here, “at a meal” (בשרותא), means at the meal — when one wants to sweeten it so that it gives a good taste, one must fill it from elsewhere, that is, fill it with spices; but for the meal to be spoiled, it spoils of itself; and this is what he said, “of the wood, from itself and in itself.” And he brings

the example of Bava ben Buta, who was of Beit Shammai and himself ruled like Beit Hillel; and likewise there, in Maaser Sheni, that Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah returned all the tithes. Hyman cites Kohelet Rabbah 9:9, where Rabbi Yitzchak called Rabbi Yehoshua son of Rabbi Tumi and Rabbi Burka “a holy congregation.” In Jerusalem Talmud Bikkurim, chapter 3, end of halakhah 3: when the Patriarch appointed unworthy judges, Yaakov of Kefar Nevuraya expounded, “And the Lord is in His holy Temple” — here is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar
in the synagogue-study-house of Caesarea (Hyman explains that he was worthy to be appointed, being a great man, and considers this undoubted evidence of a date after Rabbi Ami’s death).

SourceTanchuma has a sandal for its FOOT; the later Yerushalmi wording has a HEEL for its sandal, and both are retained distinctly. The proverb’s suppliedסבא and Beitzahסמא remain separate, with no invented cup/axehandle; Hyman explicitly interprets בשרותא as atameal and offers his own meal/spicing/spoiling explanation. NamedShabbat29b confirms Avin’s bench in a MARBLEupperroom beforeYitzchak, not a person namedShisha.

Two layers are retained: the proverb’s unresolved סבא/סמא forms, followed by Hyman’s proposed meal-and-spices interpretation. His explanation is translated on its own terms and does not supply a newly established dictionary meaning for either form.

The named digital witnesses checked for this review do not establish a single identity, teacher list, or chronology for every occurrence collected by Hyman. In Yerushalmi Ketubot13:1 the Admon formula names Rabban Gamliel in full; the supplied אר״נ remains disclosed in the inherited note. Orlah1:2 and Bavli Ketubot109a support particular Chizkiyah transmissions, while the intended Yitzchak–Chizkiyah chain at Hyman’s literal Avodah Zarah45a locator was not established in the bounded checked passages. Peah1:4 names Yitzchak ben Chakula and Yehoshua ben Levi as saying the same thing; the intended Nedarim8:1 parallel was not independently established. Neither bounded result proves absence. The Sukkah joint ruling was located at the end of digital chapter1; it does not establish joint office or Hyman’s criticism of Penei Moshe.

The consulted Yoma78a text has Tzadok ben Chakula and Rabbi Abba; Hyman supplies Chaluka and regards the proposed Yitzchak/Abbahu readings as more correct. These are his attributed corrective judgments. Yuchasin, Dikdukei Soferim, manuscript siglum א״פ, noteק, and the Constantinople and Venice printing reports were not independently collated here. Empty catalogue responses do not show that a work or reading is absent. The Tanchuma Buber Behaalotekha16 witness names Yitzchak bar Elazar of Caesarea and a sandal for its foot; the Yerushalmi Shabbat1:3 witness gives a heel for its sandal. Hoshaya barShamai/berabbiShamai in the checked Yerushalmi passages differs from Hyman’s barShimi; each form is retained.

Yerushalmi Berakhot7:3 and Megillah3:7 name Yitzchak ben/bar Elazar in the saying about the prophets’ truthfulness; Bavli Yoma69b names Rabbi Elazar. Hyman’s supplied79b locator and his report of Yaakov son of Rabbi Elazar and the abbreviation ר״י in Midrash Tehillim remain his report, without a fresh apparatus collation or identity expansion. The meal passage was located in digital Eikhah Rabbah3:6, where the name is Yitzchak berabbi Eliezer; Hyman’s Elazar form and supplied3:66 citation are preserved. Kohelet Rabbah9:9 has Timi/Burkei beside Hyman’s Tumi/Burka. The meanings of the proverb’s סבא/סמא and the reading מדרשא versus the checked מדרתא remain unresolved. The proverb and Hyman’s meal-and-spices interpretation remain separate layers. Hyman’s assertions about generations, Caesarea, pupils, and an event undoubtedly after Rabbi Ami’s death remain attributed inferences, not independently admitted biographical facts.

The earlier notes describe the review before the printed pages were consulted. Hyman, vol. II, p. 787, prints אר״ג in the Admon formula where the supplied transcription reads אר״נ. The consulted Hebrew of Jerusalem Talmud Ketubot 13:1 spells out Rabban Gamliel; its English version gives Rabban Simeon ben Gamliel. Ketubot 109a also spells out Rabban Gamliel, in the transmission by Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar in Chizkiyah’s name. Hyman’s p. 788 visibly prints א) after Rabbi Yehudah Nesia. The consulted Jerusalem Talmud passages in Ketubot 2:9, Gittin 3:4 and Eruvin 7:10 name Rabbi Yudan Nesia without Hyman’s numbering.

Hyman, vol. II, p. 788, prints the Demai locator פ״ב ה״א־ו. and the word שוריי. In Jerusalem Talmud Demai 2:1 Rabbi Mana first reports that people in Caesarea treated fig cake as exempt, then asks Rabbi Yitzchak. The consulted Hebrew writes זוגה in the ensuing answer and זוגא in the transmission about Caesarea. Guggenheimer reads the name Zeugos in both and understands the word as granting permission. The extra printed locator stays literal.

Hyman, vol. II, p. 789, prints Yoma עט: (79b). The consulted parallel is Yoma 69b, which names Rabbi Elazar. The Jerusalem Talmud parallels in Berakhot 7:3 and Megillah 3:7 name Rabbi Yitzchak ben or bar Elazar. Hyman’s proposed omitted words and his account of the Midrash Tehillim abbreviation remain his textual judgments.

The same printed page distinguishes סבא דקיסה for Maaser Sheni from סמא דקיסא for Beitzah. The consulted Jerusalem Talmud readings have סבא at Maaser Sheni 5:3, סמא at Beitzah 2:4, and ססא with an additional first-clause wording at Chagigah 2:3. These versions preserve the coal line, while the wood terms remain uncertain. The Maaser Sheni context concerns the returned tithes; the Beitzah and Chagigah contexts concern Bava ben Buta’s action. The culinary explanation in the following paragraph is Hyman’s.

Hyman, vol. II, p. 789, prints מדרשא in the description of the Caesarea synagogue. Jerusalem Talmud Bikkurim 3:3 in the consulted Hebrew reads מדרתא, rendered “fortified synagogue” by Guggenheimer, in the passage criticizing appointments made for money. The translation follows Hyman’s printed wording and leaves the type of institution specific to each witness. In Kohelet Rabbah 9:9 the consulted text names Timi and Burkei beside Hyman’s Tumi and Burka.

[Jerusalem Talmud Ketubot 13:1:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Ketubot.13.1.7) has Rabbi Ba bar Zavda transmit in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chakula. [Ketubot 109a:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Ketubot.109a.5) gives the same Admon rule with Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar citing Chizkiyah. [Jerusalem Talmud Orlah 1:2:9](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Orlah.1.2.9) names Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chakula in Chizkiyah’s name. [Seder HaDorot 2146](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=2146&lang=en) discusses several possible divisions of the names in [Pesachim 113b:18](https://www.sefaria.org/Pesachim.113b.18); Hyman argues for the division described here.

The two Jerusalem Talmud versions name Rabbi Yitzchak ben or bar Elazar. The consulted Bavli at Yoma 69b gives the shorter name Rabbi Elazar. In the separate Yoma 78a episode, the consulted Hebrew names Rabbi Tzadok ben Chakulah and Rabbi Abba. Hyman’s proposed names are Yitzchak and Abbahu.

At Avodah Zarah 48b the consulted text has Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar transmit in Chizkiyah’s name on passing under an asherah. It then gives Rabbi Yochanan’s different ruling. Hyman gives 45a for the transmission.
